When several alerts fire at once the case is the **primary anomaly** — the service the other alerts ripple from, carrying the runaway deviation: read the rows' shape before their size — a latency row that moves only its p90 is a partial-traffic ripple (only the traffic sharing a path with the degraded pod slowed), while the row whose p50 and p90 both move carries the delay across all of its traffic and marks the epicenter; among those both-percentile rows the epicenter carries the steepest p90 escalation (measured baselines only), and the graph closes it (`GetServiceDependencies`): every ripple is its direct neighbor, so a candidate that would need a quiet intermediate hop is not the source — and when two neighbors both spike from a zeroed baseline (`New Spike`, nothing to rank by), the caller's bigger number is its wait on the callee accumulated: the downstream one of the pair is the source. Percentages on near-zero baselines prove nothing. A saturation row counts only when it rides on that epicenter **and comes with the service's own latency rise** — a genuine resource fault shows the throttle *and* its own latency climbing together; a bare `cpu_cfs` row on a service that is not the epicenter, with no latency of its own, is collateral noise — don't out-rank the runaway deviation with it. **And when no latency row is in the set at all — the alerts read as bare saturation — the case is not on the saturation surface: a `Val: … (Throttled)` with no normal to compare against shows no movement (a chronically throttled value reads the same before and after), and sub-core percentages are sub-noise; the row that carries an actual deviation beyond saturation — a traffic / network move — is the one that names the service.** A `LATENCY_MISSING` row ("metrics dropped to zero/NaN") is a hole the collection left in the injection window, not a service's deviation — it never names the case, so don't anchor on it. And when a whole-system network-drop sweep carries no latency row at all, the epicenter is the point every request flows through (the system's total traffic) — its collapse is the source, the rest is the ripple.
